DECISION TREE · IN PRACTICE
Where It's Used — and Its Trade-offs
APPLICATIONS
Credit scoring rules · Medical triage / diagnosis checklists · Customer-churn flagging · Simple fraud-alert rules · Any setting where a human must read and 
approve the model's logic
MERITS
✓ Fully interpretable — you can read the exact decision path (a “white box” 
model)
✓ No feature scaling or normalisation needed
✓ Naturally handles both numeric and categorical features
✓ Cheap and fast to train and to score new records
DEMERITS
✗ Prone to overfitting — a fully grown tree can memorise noise
✗ Unstable: a small change in data can produce a very different tree
✗ Biased toward features with many distinct values/levels
✗ Poor at extrapolating beyond the range seen in training (regression)
SUPERVISED LEARNING 05 / 13

Grouping Points by Proximity
1 Choose k (the number of clusters) and initialize k centroids — e.g. as k randomly chosen data points.
2 Assignment step: assign every point to its nearest centroid, measured by Euclidean distance.
3 Update step: recompute each centroid as the mean position of all points now assigned to it.
4 Repeat the assign and update steps — points can switch clusters as the centroids shift.
5 Stop when centroids no longer move (or after a max iteration count) — the clusters have converged.
Init
(k centroids) → Assign
→ nearest centroid → Update
(mean of points) → Assign
→ nearest centroid → Converged
(stable centroids)
